newsitem.title: INDIA: Scientists pledge plan to stop spread of malaria.
newsitem.headline: Scientists pledge plan to stop spread of malaria.

text.p: Leading scientists on Wednesday pledged to adopt a plan to halt the spread of malaria over the next decade but said they would need greater financial backing to control the health menace.

The Malaria Foundation said in a statement that it had detected greater global coordination to combat the disease, which it said is spreading rapidly and kills up to three million people every year, mostly African children.

"The Malaria Foundation aims to use current international momentum to set targets to stop the spread of malaria over the next 10 years," it said in a statement released at a conference on the mosquito-borne disease in southern India.

The conference, timed to coincide with the 100th anniversary of the discovery that the disease is spread by mosquitoes, has brought together more than 700 scientists, public health officials, government agencies and industries.

The foundation, a non-profit organisation based in New York with a 50-member scientific board, said malaria was a growing public health problem which could be substantially reduced with concerted global action.

"If we go forward as a team, we can set realistic targets to reduce morbidity and mortality caused by malaria, but I should stress increased resources will be essential for this process," Malaria Foundation president Mary Galinski said.
The foundation, whose board includes scientists from more than a dozen countries, did not spell out the 10-year targets.
Experts at the five-day conference that started on Monday said relatively little money was being spent on malaria research although about 2.5 billion people are at risk in more than 90 countries.

The foundation said the United States spent $84 million on malaria research in 1993, compared with $1.5 billion every year on AIDS. But, it said, almost as many people die every year from malaria as have died in the last 15 years from AIDS.

Although malaria funding by the U.S. and British governments has recently risen, most pharmaceutical companies remain reluctant to commit large investments to a disease which has proven so difficult to control, conference delegates said.
Past efforts to fight malaria have been hampered by a lack of coordination among experts who have focused on different ways to combat the problem, none of which has wiped out the disease.

"There is an urgent need for concerted action to control malaria now before drug and insecticide resistance, population shifts and potential climatic changes combine to further expand this major worldwide public health disaster," the statement quoted Dan Colley, director of parasitic diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as saying.
